title: Bamana Empire
capsule: The Bamana (Bambara) Empire of Ségou on the middle Niger was founded around 1712 by Mamari (Biton) Coulibaly, who reorganized a youth association (tòn) into a personal standing army of slave-soldiers (tondjon), levied cowrie taxation, and built a river navy that briefly subdued Djenné, Timbuktu, and the rump Mali state. After his death in 1755 a turbulent interregnum gave way in 1766 to Ngolo Diarra, a former tondjon who founded the long-ruling Ngolossi line and restored the empire's strength; his son Mansong (r. c. 1788–1808) presided over Ségou at its height, a fortified twin-bank capital sustained by cavalry tribute and relentless slave-raiding. Imperial power waned after Mansong's death, and the Fula jihad of Seku Amadu—victorious at Noukouma in 1818 and master of the Massina region soon after—broke Bamana dominance over the inner delta, marking the end of the empire's era of supremacy by the early 1820s.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The core Bamana territory around Ségou on the middle Niger is well attested in French colonial ethnographic sources and oral tradition; peripheral tributary zones fluctuated and are imprecisely bounded.
